lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Materials Used in Making Simple Agricultural Tools

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Describe simple agricultural tools assembled from their environment.
- Identify the materials used to make these tools, and show how the parts are connected.

pages.title: What are Simple Agricultural Tools?
pages.body: Simple agricultural tools are hand operated implements, made from readily available materials, that help farmers carry out everyday farming tasks such as clearing land, digging soil, planting seeds, weeding, and harvesting crops, without relying on complex machinery. Understanding what these tools are made from, and how their parts fit together, is the first step toward being able to make, repair, or improve them.

pages.title: The Cutlass (Machete)
pages.body: A cutlass, also known as a machete, has a long, flat, sharpened steel blade attached to a wooden or plastic handle, and is used for clearing bush, cutting grass, and harvesting certain crops. The steel blade is chosen for its ability to hold a sharp cutting edge and withstand repeated impact, while the handle, often made of hardwood, provides a secure, comfortable grip.

pages.title: The Hoe
pages.body: A hoe consists of a flat or curved metal blade attached at an angle to a long wooden handle, and is used for tilling soil, weeding, and forming mounds or ridges for planting. The metal blade, usually made of steel or iron, provides the strength and durability needed to cut through soil repeatedly, while the wooden handle allows the farmer to apply force from a standing position without excessive bending.

questions.e: A cutlass, also known as a machete, has a long, flat, sharpened steel blade attached to a wooden or plastic handle, and is used for clearing bush, cutting grass, and harvesting certain crops.

questions.e: A hoe consists of a flat or curved metal blade attached at an angle to a long wooden handle, and is used for tilling soil, weeding, and forming mounds or ridges for planting.

pages.title: The Rake
pages.body: A rake typically has a row of metal or wooden teeth (tines) attached to a crossbar, which is in turn attached to a long wooden handle, and is used for gathering leaves, levelling soil, and clearing debris from a field. The teeth need to be rigid enough to move through soil or plant material without bending out of shape, while remaining light enough for the farmer to use comfortably over an extended period.

pages.title: The Sickle
pages.body:
A sickle has a short, curved steel blade attached to a short wooden handle, and is used for cutting grass, harvesting grain crops, or trimming vegetation close to the ground. The curved shape of the blade allows a farmer to gather and cut a bundle of stems in a single sweeping motion, making it especially useful for harvesting crops such as rice or millet.

[[pic:A labelled illustration showing four simple agricultural tools side by side, a cutlass with its steel blade and wooden handle labelled, a hoe with its angled blade and handle labelled, a rake with its row of teeth and crossbar labelled, and a sickle with its curved blade and short handle labelled, with a small callout on each tool pointing to where the blade is fixed to the handle.]]

Notice that despite their very different shapes and uses, all four tools share the same basic structure, a metal working part designed for a specific task, firmly attached to a handle that allows the farmer to apply force safely and effectively.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: How the Parts of These Tools Are Connected

pages.title: How the Parts of These Tools Are Connected
pages.body: Tangs and sockets, rivets, and bindings are common methods used to connect the metal working part of a tool to its handle. A tang is a narrow extension of the metal blade that is inserted into a hole drilled into the wooden handle, sometimes secured further with a metal ring called a ferrule to prevent the wood from splitting. A socket works in a similar way, but in this case, the metal part itself has a hollow section into which the wooden handle is inserted. Rivets, small metal pins, are sometimes used to further secure a blade to a handle by passing through holes drilled in both, then flattened at each end to hold them tightly together. Bindings, such as tightly wound wire, cord, or strips of leather, can also be used, especially in simpler, locally made tools, to lash a blade securely to its handle.

pages.title: Materials Available in the Local Environment
pages.body: Scrap metal from old vehicle parts or broken tools, hardwood branches, bamboo, and natural fibres such as vines or rope are examples of materials commonly available in a local environment that farmers and blacksmiths can use to assemble or repair simple agricultural tools without needing to purchase new, manufactured parts. Making practical use of these locally available materials reduces cost and makes basic tool making and repair accessible even in areas with limited access to hardware stores or specialised equipment.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Blacksmiths in many farming communities specialise in shaping and sharpening metal tool blades, often reusing and reshaping scrap metal through heating and hammering, a traditional skill that remains valuable for keeping agricultural tools in good working condition at low cost.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Processes Involved in Making Agricultural Tools

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Describe the activities and processes involved in making different agricultural tools.
- Explain the materials, processes, constraints and precautions involved in manufacturing simple agricultural tools.

pages.title: General Processes in Making Agricultural Tools
pages.body: Shaping the metal, forming the handle, connecting the parts, and finishing the tool are four general processes that apply broadly across making most simple agricultural tools, though the specific techniques used differ depending on the tool and the materials available.

pages.title: Shaping the Metal
pages.body: Shaping the metal working part of a tool, such as a hoe blade or cutlass blade, typically involves heating a piece of metal, often scrap metal, in a fire or forge until it becomes soft enough to hammer into the desired shape, then allowing it to cool. This process, called forging, requires skill and experience to judge the correct temperature and to hammer the metal evenly, and is traditionally carried out by a blacksmith.

pages.title: Forming the Handle
pages.body: Forming the handle usually involves selecting a suitable piece of hardwood, cutting it to the appropriate length, and shaping it, often by carving or sanding, so that it fits comfortably in the hand and connects properly to the metal working part of the tool. A well shaped handle reduces strain on the user's hands during repeated use.

questions.q: Forging is best described as
o: Growing crops directly
Heating and hammering metal into shape
Painting a finished tool
Planting seeds in soil
questions.e: Shaping the metal working part of a tool, such as a hoe blade or cutlass blade, typically involves heating a piece of metal, often scrap metal, in a fire or forge until it becomes soft enough to hammer into the desired shape, then allowing it to cool.

questions.q: Forming the handle of a tool typically involves
o: Heating metal until it melts completely
Ignoring the fit and comfort of the handle entirely
Selecting, cutting and shaping suitable wood
Using only metal, with no wood involved
questions.e: Forming the handle usually involves selecting a suitable piece of hardwood, cutting it to the appropriate length, and shaping it, often by carving or sanding, so that it fits comfortably in the hand and connects properly to the metal working part of the tool.

pages.title: Connecting the Parts
pages.body: Connecting the parts, using a tang and socket, rivets, or bindings, as studied in Lesson 16, is a critical stage, since a poorly connected blade can loosen or detach during use, creating a serious safety hazard. This stage often requires careful measurement and fitting, ensuring the blade sits securely and at the correct angle relative to the handle for the tool's intended purpose.

pages.title: Finishing the Tool
pages.body:
Finishing the tool typically involves sharpening the cutting edge, if applicable, smoothing any rough surfaces on the handle, and sometimes applying a protective coating, such as oil, to the metal to help prevent rust. This final stage ensures the tool is safe, comfortable, and effective to use.

[[pic:A four panel process diagram showing the manufacture of a simple hoe, the first panel showing a blacksmith heating and hammering a piece of scrap metal into a blade shape over a small forge, the second showing a carved wooden handle being shaped, the third showing the blade being fitted and secured onto the handle using a socket connection, and the fourth showing the finished hoe being sharpened and oiled.]]

Notice how each stage builds on the one before it, since a well shaped blade and a well formed handle are only useful once they are properly connected, and even a well connected tool still needs a final finishing stage to be genuinely safe and ready for use.

questions.e: Finishing the tool typically involves sharpening the cutting edge, if applicable, smoothing any rough surfaces on the handle, and sometimes applying a protective coating, such as oil, to the metal to help prevent rust.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Constraints Involved in Manufacturing Simple Agricultural Tools

pages.title: Constraints Involved in Manufacturing Simple Agricultural Tools
pages.body: Limited access to specific materials, limited access to specialised equipment such as a proper forge, and the time and skill required for careful shaping and fitting are common constraints facing anyone manufacturing simple agricultural tools, particularly in a small scale or rural setting. These constraints often mean tools are made using available scrap materials and traditional hand tools, rather than modern industrial machinery, which can affect the consistency and precision of the finished tool compared with a factory manufactured equivalent.

pages.title: Precautions Involved in Manufacturing Simple Agricultural Tools
pages.body: Wearing appropriate protective equipment, such as gloves and eye protection, when heating, hammering or sharpening metal, working in a well ventilated area when using a forge, and testing a finished tool carefully before regular use are important precautions for anyone involved in making simple agricultural tools. These precautions protect the tool maker from burns, flying metal fragments, and other injuries that can occur during the shaping, connecting, and finishing processes.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Community based tool making, often centred around a local blacksmith, remains an important, low cost source of agricultural tools in many rural areas, allowing farmers to obtain and repair tools without depending entirely on manufactured products transported from distant towns or cities.

pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Produce simple farm tools using materials from the environment.

pages.title: From Knowledge to Manufacture
pages.body: Lessons 16 and 17 built up the knowledge needed to identify suitable materials and understand the processes, constraints and precautions involved in making simple agricultural tools. This final lesson in the substrand focuses on actually producing a simple farm tool using materials from the environment, turning that accumulated knowledge into a genuine, practical skill.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Choosing a Suitable Tool to Manufacture

pages.title: Choosing a Suitable Tool to Manufacture
pages.body: Selecting a relatively simple, low risk tool to manufacture, such as a small rake, a digging stick, or a simple weeding hoe, is a sensible starting point for a first practical tool making project, since these tools generally require less specialised metalworking than a cutlass or sickle, while still providing genuine, useful experience in material selection, shaping, and assembly.

pages.title: Gathering Locally Available Materials
pages.body: Collecting suitable materials from the local environment, such as a straight, sturdy branch for a handle, or a piece of scrap metal or hard wood for a working blade, is the first practical step in manufacturing a tool, directly applying the material identification skills studied in Lesson 16. Selecting materials that are strong enough for the tool's intended purpose, yet still workable with available hand tools, is an important, practical judgement to make at this stage.

pages.title: Shaping and Assembling the Tool
pages.body:
Shaping the chosen materials, whether by carving a wooden handle, or, with appropriate adult supervision, shaping a metal working part, and then assembling the tool by connecting the working part securely to the handle, directly applies the general processes studied in Lesson 17. Careful, patient work at this stage, rather than rushing, generally produces a safer, more effective, longer lasting tool.

[[pic:A step by step photographic style sequence showing a learner manufacturing a simple weeding hoe, first selecting a straight branch and a piece of scrap metal, then shaping the branch into a handle, then fitting and securing the metal piece to the handle using a binding, and finally testing the finished tool by lightly working a small patch of soil, with a supervising adult visible in the background.]]

Notice how this practical sequence mirrors the general process studied in Lesson 17, material selection, shaping, connecting, and a final testing and finishing stage, now applied to an actual, learner made tool.

pages.title: Testing and Finishing the Manufactured Tool
pages.body: Testing a newly manufactured tool on a small, controlled task, such as lightly working a small patch of soil with a homemade hoe, allows any weaknesses, such as a loose connection or an uncomfortable handle, to be identified and corrected before the tool is used more extensively. Making small adjustments after this initial test, such as tightening a binding or smoothing a rough edge, reflects the same finishing process studied in Lesson 17, applied directly to your own manufactured tool.

pages.title: Safety During Manufacturing
pages.body: Working under appropriate adult supervision, particularly for any step involving cutting, heating or sharpening metal, wearing suitable protective equipment such as gloves, and working carefully and patiently rather than rushing, are essential safety practices throughout the manufacturing process, directly applying the precautions studied in Lesson 17 to this hands on activity.

pages.body:

Successfully manufacturing even a single, simple agricultural tool provides valuable, transferable experience relevant well beyond agriculture, including practical problem solving, careful material selection, and an appreciation for the effort and skill involved in producing tools that might otherwise be taken for granted when simply purchased ready made.
